reasoning: This is a narrative literature review synthesizing existing research on schizophrenia cognitive impairment, pathophysiology, and treatment. It does not report generation or use of research software, nor does it generate or analyze a specific research dataset - it summarizes findings from numerous prior studies without creating new software or data artifacts.

This is a narrative/consensus guideline paper that synthesizes existing published literature (systematic reviews, case reports, case series, and prior studies) to produce clinical recommendations for managing catatonia. It does not generate or use any research software - no code, tools, or computational workflows are described or employed. It also does not generate new research data or substantively analyze an existing dataset; rather, it reviews and cites findings from other studies' data without performing new data analysis of its own. The core work consists of literature review, expert consensus, and formulation of graded clinical recommendations, which falls under 'Other' research artefacts (documentation/guideline) rather than software or data as defined in the criteria.

The study uses existing research software (TopoToolbox V2) to process a nationwide DEM, applying standard flow-routing algorithms - this is use of existing software (not creating/extending it), so S2. The research generates a novel national-scale geodatabase of 91 morphometric/topographic characteristics for 128 catchments, creating substantive new research data (stream network and catchment attribute datasets) made accessible via an ArcGIS web-application - this is clearly D1, data generated through the research that produces new knowledge about Philippine river catchments.

The paper develops a new application of the Jaya algorithm (with LHS enhancement) for graph drawing, implemented in a newly created visualization tool (MGDrawVis), constituting generated research software that produces new knowledge (comparative performance results). It also generates new research data: synthetic graph datasets (Erdős–Rényi random graphs) across multiple experimental phases and scalability tests, which are created specifically for this study (though real-world graphs like dolphins, karate club, etc. were also used, these are existing benchmark data used alongside newly generated random graphs). Since software and data are both generated as part of the research (with code and data deposited on OSF), this falls under S1D1.

This is a study protocol for a planned randomised controlled trial that has not yet generated or analysed results. It describes planned use of standard tools (R for random number generation, REDCap for data capture) as routine utilities rather than research software generating new knowledge, and no actual research data (questionnaire/task results) have been collected or analysed yet - only planned data collection procedures are described. Since this is a protocol describing future data collection and standard administrative software usage, it falls under S3D3 (no research software generated/used for creating new knowledge, no research data yet generated or used).

This study generated new survey data (quantitative Likert-scale surveys and qualitative interviews/thematic analysis) from four cohorts of nurses and midwives (n=153) collected specifically for this research, which is novel research data used to generate new knowledge about genomics competencies. No research software was created or used substantively; data collection used commercial survey tools (SurveyMonkey, Jisc Online Surveys) and standard analysis in Microsoft Excel/statistical tests, which are utility tools rather than research software developed for the study.

This is an editorial/introduction to a special issue, summarizing and reviewing seven accepted papers. It does not itself generate or use any research software or data; it only describes (secondhand) what the reviewed papers did. No software was created or used by the editors, and no new data was generated or analyzed in this editorial itself.

The study uses existing software tools (NiftyReg for registration, Varian Eclipse TPS for treatment planning) as utilities rather than developing new research software, so it falls under S2 (software used, generating new knowledge through analysis). On the data side, the researchers collected a new cohort of 10 GBM patients' DW-MRI/ADC maps, CT scans, and derived cell density/TCP maps specifically for this research, generating novel patient-specific datasets (cell density maps, TCP maps, BTV volumes, SIB dose plans) that did not exist before and were essential to producing the paper's findings. This constitutes substantive data generation (D1), which supersedes any data use classification per the general rule that generation implies use.

The study developed an "innovative" digital image analysis/phenotyping workflow (with novel techniques like dynamic image thresholding and colocalisation-based resolution of double-positive cells) implemented in open-source software, which was essential to generating the novel single-cell phenotype classifications - this constitutes generated research software that produced new knowledge (not just a routine utility). The study also generated new primary research data: a cohort of multiplexed immunofluorescence images (NLPHL, THRLBCL, LRcHL, tonsil cases) with millions of phenotyped cell detections, which is the substantive, newly collected data underlying the paper's novel biological findings. Both software and data were generated specifically for this research and were central to producing new knowledge, satisfying S1 and D1 criteria.

The researchers manually coded all steps of the GMDH neural network in MATLAB from scratch (since no toolbox existed for GMDH), implementing training, validation, and testing phases themselves - this constitutes research software generation that produced new knowledge (feature selection results, burnout classification). The data used (questionnaire responses from 384 startup directors/representatives) was explicitly reused from a previous study [31], not newly generated in this paper - the methods of sampling and data collection are detailed in that prior article. Thus this paper uses existing substantive data while generating new research software (the custom GMDH implementation).

The paper reports new experimental data generated by the researchers themselves: a novel crystal structure of Mcl-1 bound to AMG-176 (deposited in PDB as 8AV9), NMR spectroscopy data (15N-HSQC, NOE, chemical shift measurements for free-in-solution conformer analysis), and binding/potency assays (SPR, FRET, cellular EC50). This constitutes substantive new research data that directly generates new knowledge about Mcl-1 plasticity and inhibitor preorganization, qualifying as D1 (Data Generated). Regarding software, the paper uses standard computational tools for scoring (PP, PLB index methods), MD simulations, and DFT calculations, as well as NMR structure calculation software - these are established research software/tools used as utilities to analyze the generated data, not software whose development or extension constitutes a core contribution of the paper. No new software is created or significantly extended; existing computational methods are applied as routine analysis tools. Thus this falls under S3 (No Research Software) since the software used functions as a utility rather than being the source of new knowledge itself - the new knowledge comes from the experimental data (crystal structures, NMR data) rather than from any novel software development.

This is a cluster RCT where the researchers collected original data (maternal/child health outcomes, demographics, anthropometric measurements) from 873 pregnant women across 8 clinics in rural South Africa, generating new substantive research data (D1). For software, they used existing statistical tools (R's blme package) for standard mixed-effects model analysis - this is a routine statistical utility rather than research software created or substantially extended for the study, so it falls under S3 (no research software generated, existing software used only as a utility for analysis).

The study uses existing EHR databases (CPRD Gold and UK Biobank linked primary care records) and applies standard statistical software (Poisson models) to analyze them - no new research software/tool was created; the Poisson modelling and phenotype code lists are analysis methodology rather than generated research software. The paper does develop new codelists/phenotypes (symptom and blood test code lists) which could be seen as a data artifact, but the core contribution is the use of existing substantive datasets (CPRD and UK Biobank EHRs linked to cancer registry data) to generate new epidemiological knowledge about symptom recording differences. Since the underlying research data (patient records) were not created by the researchers but obtained from existing data sources, and the phenotype codelists are best seen as a classification scheme (not a primary research dataset) rather than a new substantive dataset, this is classified as 'Data Used' (D2). No new research software was generated — only existing statistical methods/software were used to analyze the data, so S3.

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum. It is a narrative review/discussion drawing on existing literature, frameworks, and historical examples, without generating or using any research software, and without generating or using research data (no datasets, surveys, or empirical analyses conducted). Hence it falls under no software and no data.

This is a data descriptor paper presenting DOCU-CLIM, a newly compiled global dataset of 621 documentary climate time series, including rescued/digitized historical records not previously available electronically. This clearly constitutes generated research data (D1). While the authors used statistical regression (forward models) and existing climate datasets (BEST, HadCRUT5, GPCC) for evaluation, these are standard statistical utilities rather than research software created or substantively extended for the study, and no specific software tool is described as being generated or used as a novel research artifact—only an R-code snippet for reading files is mentioned as supplementary material, which is incidental/utility rather than substantive research software generating new knowledge. Hence S3 (no substantive research software) and D1 (data generated).

The study generated novel research data: a 100-year dated sedimentary archive from Lake Ring was sampled and subjected to multilocus eDNA metabarcoding, mass spectrometry quantification of DDT, and compiled with climate/biocide records, producing new biodiversity and chemical datasets that did not exist before (clear D1). For software, the researchers used existing established tools and pipelines (QIIME2, DADA2, PICRUST2, ANCOM, cutadapt, FASTQC, multiqc, ggplot2, pheatmap, sklearn classifiers) and statistical methods (sCCA, PERMANOVA) to analyze their data, but did not create or substantially extend any new software/tool themselves - these are utility applications of existing research software to generate new scientific knowledge (S2), not creation of new software artifacts.

This is a narrative/state-of-the-art literature review discussing BBB imaging techniques (PET, SPECT, DCE-MRI, ASL, CT) across various neurological diseases. It does not generate or use any specific research software (no new code, scripts, or computational tools are developed or applied in the research itself), nor does it generate or analyze a specific dataset. It synthesizes prior literature and knowledge rather than reporting new data collection or software development/application. Hence it falls under No Software, No Data.

This is a cross-sectional survey study where the researchers collected new primary data (survey of 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia) on COVID-19 knowledge, vaccine willingness, and vaccine uptake, generating substantive new research data. For software, they used STATA 17.1 for statistical analysis and KoboToolbox as a data collection app - both are existing standard tools/utilities used for routine purposes (data collection and statistical analysis) rather than research software created or substantively extended as part of the research itself. No new software was developed, and the existing software used (STATA, KoboToolbox) functions as a utility rather than generating new knowledge itself. Hence this falls under S3 (No Research Software) and D1 (Research Substantive Data Generated).

This is a narrative review article discussing existing literature on GWAS, post-GWAS methods, and microglia biology in AD and PD. It synthesizes findings from numerous previously published studies but does not generate new software, use existing software/tools to produce new analyses of its own, generate new datasets, or analyze existing datasets itself. It only describes and discusses tools (e.g., FUMA, MAGMA, DeepSea, CADD) and datasets used in the cited studies, not by the authors of this review. No new research artefacts (software or data) are produced or substantively used by the authors in this paper itself.

This is a narrative literature review summarizing existing research on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it create or analyze new research data; it synthesizes findings from previously published studies (referenced by citation numbers) without conducting new experiments, software development, or data generation/analysis itself.

The paper develops a novel counterfactual GAN (a new research software/neural network architecture adapted and extended from Choi et al.'s framework) specifically created for this research to synthesize counterfactual OCT images modeling retinal aging - this constitutes generated research software that produces new knowledge (novel insights into subject-specific retinal aging trajectories). The underlying OCT imaging data comes from the pre-existing UK Biobank population study, which is used (not generated) as training/testing data for the models - this is existing substantive research data that is used to generate new findings, qualifying as D2.

The researchers used existing pretrained models (GPT-2, Word2Vec, GloVe, fastText, sentence-transformer models) as tools/software to generate simulated narratives and compute NLP metrics - these are existing research software used rather than newly created software (though they built an analysis pipeline, it's primarily leveraging existing models and libraries, plus they provide a tutorial but don't claim to have created new software as a contribution). They generated substantial new data: simulated FTD-like narratives (using parameter perturbations) and clinical ratings of these narratives, which is novel research data created specifically for this study and used to validate NLP metrics - this constitutes generated research data (D1).

This is a study protocol describing a planned future survey (not yet conducted). No actual data has been collected or analyzed yet - it's all prospective ("will be distributed", "will be collected"). The only software mentioned is Qualtrics XM, a commercial survey platform used as a utility tool rather than research software developed or substantively used to generate new knowledge. Since the survey has not been administered yet and no data exists at time of writing, this falls under 'no data' (planned/proposed artefacts don't count). Thus S3D3.

This is a phase 1 clinical trial paper reporting new pharmacokinetic/safety data generated from two original drug-drug interaction studies in healthy subjects (new clinical data constituting research data generated, D1). Software used includes Phoenix WinNonlin for noncompartmental PK analysis and SAS for statistical analysis, which are existing established research software tools used as utilities to analyze the new data, not created or substantially extended by the researchers (S2, since these tools are used for generating the analysis/knowledge but not generated by the study). Since data was generated, the paper falls into the generated data category combined with used software, i.e., S2D1.

This paper describes methodology to operationalise a standardised scoring system using existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, dietary, physical activity data) to generate new derived variables (adherence scores) for 158,415 and 314,616 participants. This represents substantive generation of new research data (the adherence scores) derived from existing UK Biobank data - a novel dataset/measure created through this research that didn't exist before. No research software is described as being generated or used in a substantive way that creates new knowledge; the calculations involve standard statistical processing (means, sums, classification according to existing rules) rather than development or use of research software tools that themselves generate new knowledge. Thus this fits No Software, Data Generated (S3D1).

This is a narrative literature review that appraises existing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, risk scores, and ocular imaging studies reported by other researchers. The paper does not generate or use any research software itself (it discusses software/imaging systems like Brennan et al.'s app as part of the literature being reviewed, not as something the authors created or applied), nor does it generate or analyse any new research data. No new datasets, experiments, or software tools are produced or substantively used by the authors themselves; the paper is purely a synthesis/review of prior findings.

The study uses existing Google Trends data (search volume for "monkeypox") and CDC case data, both of which are external, pre-existing data sources used (not generated) for analysis - this constitutes D2 (substantive data used). For analysis, they used existing statistical software, the "Joinpoint Regression Programme" (version 4.6.0.0), an established tool used to perform joinpoint regression analysis - this is existing research software used to generate new knowledge about search trends, fitting S2 (software used). No new software or datasets were created by the authors; they only used Google Trends and CDC data retrieval and applied existing statistical software to analyze it.

This is a qualitative study using in-depth interviews with 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers in Fiji, transcribed manually and analyzed through thematic analysis. The research generated new primary qualitative data (interview transcripts) which were analyzed to derive themes and codes - this constitutes substantive data generation (D1). No research software was created or used in a substantive sense; data analysis was done manually (manual thematic analysis, transcription into Microsoft Word), with no mention of any specialized research software tools that generated new knowledge - thus S3 (No Research Software).

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that used existing published studies/data (from 76 articles and 2 national surveys like DHS and the National Micronutrient Survey) - it did not generate new primary data itself but synthesized and meta-analyzed existing data, which counts as Data Used (D2). For software, they used STATA version 17 to conduct the meta-analysis (random effects model, forest plots), which is existing research software used to produce new knowledge (pooled prevalence estimates), making it Software Used (S2) rather than S1 (no new software created) or S3 (STATA was integral/substantive to generating the meta-analytic results, not just incidental).

This study collected new empirical data (HD-EMG and force measurements) from 18 children (TD vs DCD) during handgrip tasks, decomposed into motor unit firing characteristics - this is clearly newly generated research data (D1). For software, the paper uses existing commercial/established tools (NeuroMap/PD-III decomposition algorithm by Delsys, EMGworks, Labchart, PsychoPy for audio cues, and a 'bespoke Matlab script' for force data extraction). The Matlab script and PsychoPy script are used as utility tools for data acquisition/triggering and basic extraction rather than being a novel research software contribution that itself generates new knowledge - they are incidental/utility software to support data collection and analysis, not the focus of the research or a generated artifact described in detail as a contribution. No new software is described as created/extended as a research output; existing software/algorithms (PD-III, NeuroMap) are used as tools. Thus this falls under S3 (No Research Software, just utility use) combined with D1 (Data Generated).
